title: Gene Tierney
wiki_lead:
Gene Eliza Tierney (November 19, 1920 – November 6, 1991) was an American stage and film actress. Tierney was a prominent leading lady during the Golden Age of Hollywood. She starred as Laura Hunt in Otto Preminger's Laura (1944), a film noir classic, and as Ellen Berent in John M. Stahl's Leave Her to Heaven (1945), which earned her a nomination for the Academy Award for Best Actress. Darryl F. Zanuck, co-founder of 20th Century Fox, said Tierney was "unquestionably, the most beautiful woman in movie history."
Tierney was a 20th Century Fox contract player who did much of her work for the studio. She starred in many commercially successful Fox films, including The Return of Frank James (1940; her film debut), Tobacco Road (1941), Son of Fury: The Story of Benjamin Blake (1942), Heaven Can Wait (1943), A Bell for Adano (1945), The Razor's Edge (1946), The Ghost and Mrs. Muir (1947), The Iron Curtain (1948), Whirlpool and Night and the City (both 1950), The Mating Season (1951), On the Riviera (1951), The Egyptian (1954), The Left Hand of God (1955), and The Pleasure Seekers (1964; her last film role). After her Hollywood career began to decline, Tierney made sporadic appearances on many television shows. Her role in the miniseries Scruples (1980), marked her last work credit.

Early life
Tierney was born in Brooklyn, New York, the daughter of Howard Sherwood Tierney and Belle Lavinia Tierney (née Taylor). She was named after a beloved uncle, who died young. She had an elder brother and a younger sister. Her father was a successful insurance broker of Irish descent on his paternal side; their mother was a former physical education instructor.
She attended St. Margaret's School for Girls in Waterbury, Connecticut (which merged into what became Chase Collegiate School) and Unquowa School in Fairfield, Connecticut. Tierney spent two years in Europe, attending Brillantmont International School in Lausanne, Switzerland, where she learned to speak fluent French. She returned to the US in 1936 and attended Miss Porter's School in Farmington, Connecticut. On a family trip to the West Coast, she visited Warner Bros. studios, where her mother's cousin worked as a producer of historical short films. Director Anatole Litvak, taken by the 17-year-old's beauty, told Tierney that she should become an actress. Warner Bros. wanted to sign her to a contract, but her parents advised against it because of the relatively low salary; they also wanted her to take her position in society.
Tierney's society debut occurred on September 24, 1938, when she was 17 years old. Quickly bored with society life, she decided to pursue an acting career. Her father said, "If Gene is to be an actress, it should be in the legitimate theatre." grok_lead: Gene Eliza Tierney (November 19, 1920 â November 6, 1991) was an American film and stage actress renowned for her ethereal beauty and poised performances in classic Hollywood cinema during the 1940s and 1950s. Born in Brooklyn, New York, to affluent parents Howard Sherwood Tierney, an insurance broker, and Belle Lavinia Taylor, a former physical education teacher, Tierney grew up in a privileged environment, attending elite schools including St. Margaret's in Waterbury, Connecticut, Miss Porter's School in Farmington, Connecticut, and a finishing school in Lausanne, Switzerland. After briefly studying at Columbia University and modeling in New York, she began her stage career on Broadway in 1938 with a small role in What a Life!, gaining notice in The Primrose Path (1939), which led to a contract with 20th Century Fox in 1940. Tierney's film career flourished with early supporting roles in pictures like The Return of Frank James (1940) directed by Fritz Lang and Tobacco Road (1941), but she achieved stardom with her titular role in Otto Preminger's Laura (1944), a film noir thriller that showcased her enigmatic allure and earned her widespread acclaim as one of Hollywood's most beautiful actresses. Her performance as the obsessive Ellen Berent in Leave Her to Heaven (1945), a Technicolor psychological drama, brought her the only Academy Award nomination of her career for Best Actress, highlighting her ability to convey subtle emotional depth beneath a glamorous facade. Other notable films include Dragonwyck (1946), a gothic romance with Vincent Price; The Ghost and Mrs. Muir (1947), a supernatural fantasy opposite Rex Harrison; and film noirs such as Whirlpool (1949) and Where the Sidewalk Ends (1950), both directed by Preminger, where she excelled in portraying vulnerable yet resilient women. Over her two-decade screen career, Tierney appeared in more than 30 films, often under the guidance of directors like John Ford and Josef von Sternberg, and her styleâmarked by a soft-spoken delivery, refined elegance, and an air of quiet intensityâinfluenced the archetype of the mysterious Hollywood heroine. Beyond her professional success, Tierney's personal life was marked by significant challenges that impacted her career. She married costume designer Oleg Cassini in 1941, with whom she had two daughters: Daria, born in 1943 with severe disabilities including deafness and intellectual impairment due to Tierney contracting German measles during pregnancy, and Christina, born in 1948. The strain of Daria's condition, which required institutionalization, contributed to Tierney's battles with clinical depression and manic-depressive illness, leading to multiple hospitalizations, including electroconvulsive therapy at the Menninger Clinic in the 1950s; these health struggles caused her to take extended breaks from acting, effectively halting her momentum as a leading lady by the mid-1950s. Tierney divorced Cassini in 1952 and later married Texas oilman W. Howard Lee in 1960, a union that lasted until his death in 1981 and provided her stability during her later years. She resumed sporadic work in the 1960s, including roles in Advise and Consent (1962) and her final film, The Pleasure Seekers (1964), before retiring to Houston, Texas, where she focused on writing her 1979 autobiography, Self-Portrait: Life of a Hollywood Star. Tierney died of emphysema in Houston at age 70, leaving a legacy as a symbol of classic Hollywood glamour tempered by profound personal resilience.
